items.stem: Which of these is NOT controlled by homeostasis in humans?
items.answer: Eye colour
items.markingKey: D. Eye colour is genetically determined and not regulated.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a receptor and an effector.
items.answer: A receptor detects a stimulus; an effector (muscle or gland) produces the response.
items.markingKey: A receptor detects a stimulus; an effector (muscle or gland) produces the response. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between negative feedback and positive feedback.
items.answer: Negative feedback reverses a change to restore the set point; positive feedback amplifies a change, e.g. oxytocin increasing contractions during childbirth.
items.markingKey: Negative feedback reverses a change to restore the set point; positive feedback amplifies a change, e.g. oxytocin increasing contractions during childbirth. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Ingrid is investigating how the duration of exercise affects the time taken for heart rate to return to its resting value. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If exercise lasts longer, then recovery time will increase, because more CO₂ and lactic acid build up, so negative feedback takes longer to restore normal blood conditions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If exercise lasts longer, then recovery time will increase, because more CO₂ and lactic acid build up, so negative feedback takes longer to restore normal blood conditions.

items.stem: Amara plans an investigation into how the duration of exercise affects the time taken for heart rate to return to its resting value. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (duration of exercise (min, e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 min of step-ups)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.

items.answer: homeostasis

items.stem: Briefly explain why a fever above 42 °C is dangerous.
items.answer: Very high temperatures denature enzymes and proteins in cells, especially in the brain, so vital reactions stop.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Very high temperatures denature enzymes and proteins in cells, especially in the brain, so vital reactions stop. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Jonas writes: "Homeostasis keeps every factor in the body exactly constant." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Factors fluctuate within narrow limits around a set point.
items.markingKey: Factors fluctuate within narrow limits around a set point. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe the general features of a negative feedback system using the control of body temperature as an example, and explain what would happen if the response continued after the set point had been reached.
items.answer: Stimulus (temperature rises) → receptors (thermoreceptors in hypothalamus/skin) → coordination centre (hypothalamus) → effectors (sweat glands, arterioles) → response (cooling) → temperature returns to 37 °C and response stops. If it continued, temperature would overshoot below the set point (hypothermia), triggering the opposite responses – fluctuation.
items.markingKey: Stimulus (temperature rises) → receptors (thermoreceptors in hypothalamus/skin) → coordination centre (hypothalamus) → effectors (sweat glands, arterioles) → response (cooling) → temperature returns to 37 °C and response stops. If it continued, temperature would overshoot below the set point (hypothermia), triggering the opposite responses – fluctuation.

items.stem: Define the term "myelin sheath".
items.answer: A fatty insulating layer around some axons that speeds up the transmission of impulses

items.answer: Neurotransmitter is released only from the presynaptic neurone and receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane.

items.answer: In a reflex the impulse passes through only a few neurones and synapses via the spinal cord or lower brain, without conscious processing in the cerebral cortex.

items.stem: A student touches a hot pan and pulls her hand away before feeling pain. Describe the pathway of the impulse in this reflex arc, explaining what happens at each synapse, and explain why the pain is felt slightly after the hand moves.
items.answer: Heat receptors in the skin are stimulated; impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord; at the synapse neurotransmitter diffuses across and triggers an impulse in a relay neurone; then across a second synapse into a motor neurone; impulse reaches the biceps (effector), which contracts. Pain is felt later because a separate impulse must travel up the spinal cord to the brain and be processed in the cortex.
items.markingKey: Heat receptors in the skin are stimulated; impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord; at the synapse neurotransmitter diffuses across and triggers an impulse in a relay neurone; then across a second synapse into a motor neurone; impulse reaches the biceps (effector), which contracts. Pain is felt later because a separate impulse must travel up the spinal cord to the brain and be processed in the cortex.

It rises, and insulin is secreted to bring it down
It rises, and glucagon is secreted

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that a sugar tax on soft drinks is the best way to reduce type 2 diabetes.
items.answer: A sugar tax helps but is not enough alone; it works best with education, exercise programmes and food labelling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reduces sugar intake (e.g. Mexico’s 2014 tax cut purchases by about 7-12%); manufacturers reformulate drinks with less sugar (UK 2018 levy); revenue can fund health education. Arguments against: affects poorer people more; people may switch to other sugary foods; inactivity and genetics are also major causes. Supported judgement: A sugar tax helps but is not enough alone; it works best with education, exercise programmes and food labelling.

items.stem: Briefly describe kidney dialysis and explain what it reveals about the role of the kidneys in water and waste balance.

State the volume of drink at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.

items.stem: With reference to rising rates of type 2 diabetes in the Gulf states, explain how it illustrates lifestyle risk factors for type 2 diabetes.
items.answer: Countries such as Kuwait and Qatar have adult diabetes rates of around 20%, linked to rapid changes in diet and inactive lifestyles. Obesity and inactivity reduce the response of cells to insulin, so blood glucose is not controlled.
items.markingKey: Context (Countries such as Kuwait and Qatar have adult diabetes rates of around 20%, linked to rapid changes in diet and inactive lifestyles.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Obesity and inactivity reduce the response of cells to insulin, so blood glucose is not controlled. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to lifestyle risk factors for type 2 diabetes.

items.stem: "Homeostasis keeps every factor in the body exactly constant." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Factors fluctuate within narrow limits around a set point.
items.markingKey: Factors fluctuate within narrow limits around a set point. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which kidney dialysis shows the role of the kidneys in water and waste balance.
items.answer: Patients with kidney failure are connected to a dialysis machine 3 times a week; blood flows past a partially permeable membrane with dialysis fluid on the other side. The machine removes urea and excess water and salts by diffusion, replacing what failed kidneys can no longer do.
items.markingKey: Context (Patients with kidney failure are connected to a dialysis machine 3 times a week; blood flows past a partially permeable membrane with dialysis fluid on the other side.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The machine removes urea and excess water and salts by diffusion, replacing what failed kidneys can no longer do. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of the kidneys in water and waste balance.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Brain–computer interfaces (implants that read neurone signals) should be developed to help people with paralysis."
items.answer: The benefits for people with severe paralysis are significant, but strict ethical oversight and data protection are essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: can restore communication and movement (e.g. controlling a cursor or robotic arm); improve independence. Arguments against: surgical risks and infection; privacy of neural data; high cost; long-term effects unknown. Supported judgement: The benefits for people with severe paralysis are significant, but strict ethical oversight and data protection are essential.

items.stem: "A sugar tax on soft drinks is the best way to reduce type 2 diabetes." Discuss.
items.answer: A sugar tax helps but is not enough alone; it works best with education, exercise programmes and food labelling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reduces sugar intake (e.g. Mexico’s 2014 tax cut purchases by about 7-12%); manufacturers reformulate drinks with less sugar (UK 2018 levy); revenue can fund health education. Arguments against: affects poorer people more; people may switch to other sugary foods; inactivity and genetics are also major causes. Supported judgement: A sugar tax helps but is not enough alone; it works best with education, exercise programmes and food labelling. items.stem: "Wearable devices that monitor body temperature and heart rate will greatly improve people’s health." Discuss.
items.answer: They can help, especially for people at risk, but accuracy, privacy and access limit the benefit.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: early warning of fever or abnormal heart rhythm; encourage healthy behaviour; useful data for doctors. Arguments against: data may be inaccurate; privacy concerns; can cause anxiety; expensive for many people. Supported judgement: They can help, especially for people at risk, but accuracy, privacy and access limit the benefit. items.stem: "Kidney transplants are a better treatment than dialysis for kidney failure." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: A transplant is usually better for suitable patients, but dialysis remains essential while waiting or when transplant is not possible.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the patient can live normally without dialysis sessions; cheaper over many years; better quality of life and survival. Arguments against: shortage of donor kidneys; long waiting lists; risk of rejection; lifelong immunosuppressant drugs; surgery risks. Supported judgement: A transplant is usually better for suitable patients, but dialysis remains essential while waiting or when transplant is not possible. items.stem: Where are relay neurones found?
options: In the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord)
items.answer: In the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord)

items.stem: Which organ secretes insulin?
items.answer: Pancreas
items.markingKey: C. Beta cells in the islets of the pancreas secrete insulin.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A cell or organ that detects a stimulus (a change in the environment)"?
items.answer: receptor
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of receptor.

items.stem: Sana writes: "Shivering is a sign that the body has stopped controlling its temperature." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Shivering is an active homeostatic response: rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration.
items.markingKey: Shivering is an active homeostatic response: rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Nerve impulses travel across synapses as electricity." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Electrical impulses travel along neurones, but across a synapse the signal is chemical (neurotransmitter diffusion).
items.markingKey: Electrical impulses travel along neurones, but across a synapse the signal is chemical (neurotransmitter diffusion). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between glucagon and insulin.
items.answer: Insulin is released when blood glucose is high and lowers it (glucose → glycogen); glucagon is released when blood glucose is low and raises it (glycogen → glucose).
items.markingKey: Insulin is released when blood glucose is high and lowers it (glucose → glycogen); glucagon is released when blood glucose is low and raises it (glycogen → glucose). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why negative feedback keeps a factor close to the set point rather than at exactly one value.
items.answer: The response only starts once a change is detected and it may overshoot, so the factor fluctuates in a narrow range around the set point.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The response only starts once a change is detected and it may overshoot, so the factor fluctuates in a narrow range around the set point. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a reflex action and a voluntary action.
items.answer: A reflex is automatic, rapid and does not involve conscious thought; a voluntary action is consciously decided in the brain and is slower.
items.markingKey: A reflex is automatic, rapid and does not involve conscious thought; a voluntary action is consciously decided in the brain and is slower. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Sofia’s blood glucose was 4.9 mmol/dm³ before breakfast. It rose to 8.8 mmol/dm³ at 45 min after eating and fell to 4.8 mmol/dm³ at 105 min. (a) Calculate the mean rate of rise and the mean rate of fall in mmol/dm³ per minute. (b) Name the hormone responsible for the fall and explain how it works.
items.answer: (a) rise 0.087, fall 0.067 mmol/dm³ per min (b) insulin – cells take up glucose and the liver stores it as glycogen
items.markingKey: (a) M1 change ÷ time; A1 rise (8.8 − 4.9)/45 = 0.087; A1 fall (8.8 − 4.8)/60 = 0.067. (b) 1 insulin from the pancreas; 1 glucose taken into cells/converted to glycogen.

items.stem: Briefly describe a thermostat-controlled home heating system and explain what it reveals about negative feedback.
items.answer: When the room cools below 20 °C the thermostat switches the boiler on; when it warms above 20 °C it switches off. Like the hypothalamus, the thermostat detects deviation from a set point and triggers a response that reverses it.
items.markingKey: Context (When the room cools below 20 °C the thermostat switches the boiler on; when it warms above 20 °C it switches off.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Like the hypothalamus, the thermostat detects deviation from a set point and triggers a response that reverses it. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to negative feedback.

items.stem: A student claims that ADH makes you produce more urine. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: ADH increases water reabsorption, so less, more concentrated urine is produced.
items.markingKey: ADH increases water reabsorption, so less, more concentrated urine is produced. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using multiple sclerosis (MS) as an example, explain the role of the myelin sheath.
items.answer: The immune system damages the myelin sheaths of neurones in the brain and spinal cord. Without myelin, impulses travel more slowly or are blocked, causing problems with movement, vision and balance.
items.markingKey: Context (The immune system damages the myelin sheaths of neurones in the brain and spinal cord.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Without myelin, impulses travel more slowly or are blocked, causing problems with movement, vision and balance. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of the myelin sheath.

items.stem: "Glucagon is the substance stored in the liver." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Glycogen is stored in the liver; glucagon is the hormone that triggers its breakdown.
items.markingKey: Glycogen is stored in the liver; glucagon is the hormone that triggers its breakdown. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using marathon runners in hot conditions (e.g. Doha 2019 World Championships) as an example, explain the limits of homeostasis.
items.answer: Many runners did not finish the night-time women’s marathon at over 30 °C and high humidity; several needed medical treatment for heat exhaustion. Sweating could not remove heat fast enough in humid air, so core temperature rose beyond the range that homeostasis could correct.
items.markingKey: Context (Many runners did not finish the night-time women’s marathon at over 30 °C and high humidity; several needed medical treatment for heat exhaustion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Sweating could not remove heat fast enough in humid air, so core temperature rose beyond the range that homeostasis could correct. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limits of homeostasis.

items.stem: Outline one way in which hypothermia in mountain climbers on Everest shows the limits of thermoregulation.
items.answer: In extreme cold and wind, climbers lose heat faster than the body can generate it; core temperature drops below 35 °C, causing confusion and slowed heart rate. Vasoconstriction and shivering cannot match the heat lost, so the negative feedback fails.
items.markingKey: Context (In extreme cold and wind, climbers lose heat faster than the body can generate it; core temperature drops below 35 °C, causing confusion and slowed heart rate.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Sana plans an investigation into how the surface area to volume ratio of a “model animal” (flask or tube of hot water) affects its rate of cooling. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (size of container (and so surface area to volume ratio)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.
